analysis.one_liner: Requires colleges to publish how they handle sexual assault cases, coordinate with police, and face federal fines.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to strengthen how colleges handle campus sexual assault drew 17 cosponsors and a December 2014 hearing, then died without ever getting a committee or floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every college that gets federal student aid to sign formal agreements with local police about investigating campus sexual violence, designate confidential advisors for victims, publish annual counts of how sexual assault cases were investigated and resolved, and survey students yearly about their experiences. Colleges that failed to comply could face fines up to 1% of their operating budget. It was referred to the Senate education committee, held a subcommittee hearing, and never moved further before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future college students, especially victims of sexual assault, who would get confidential advisors, published case-disposition data, hotlines and rape-kit resources on every school's website, amnesty for good-faith reports, and an annual public survey showing how widespread the problem is on each named campus.

how_it_helps.text: Every college receiving federal funds would have to designate confidential advisors — trained, victim-centered staff who are not required to report the victim to school or police — and tell victims their full range of options.

Schools would have to publish, by name, how many sexual offense cases were investigated, referred to discipline or police, found responsible or not responsible, and what sanctions were imposed — giving students and families real data instead of opaque statistics.

The Education Department would run a standardized annual student survey on sexual violence and publish campus-level results for each named school, and could fine colleges up to $150,000 per violation for failing to report or complete the survey.
Students who report sexual violence in good faith would be protected from being punished for related conduct violations, such as underage drinking.
Federal grants for campus anti-violence programs would rise from a $300,000 to a $500,000 minimum, and could pay for training campus staff in trauma-informed forensic interviewing.

analysis.who_pays: Colleges and universities, which would bear compliance costs, mandatory memoranda of understanding with local police, required confidential advisors and training, and civil penalties of up to 1% of their operating budget for violations.

drawbacks.text: The penalty structure is steep: colleges could be fined up to 1% of their annual operating budget each year for failing to meet the law-enforcement coordination or survivor-support requirements, a burden that falls hardest on small institutions.

Schools would have to run a single uniform disciplinary process for sexual violence cases that cannot vary by a student's status, such as athletic-team membership — a requirement some educators worried could constrain campus-specific handling of cases.

Requiring large amounts of case-level reporting and annual surveys imposes real administrative work, even though the bill directs federal technical assistance and forbids statistics that identify victims or the accused.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to students — confidential advisors, published case outcomes, annual named-campus survey data, and real fines for schools that hide or mishandle assaults — are concrete and address a documented gap in campus accountability. The costs are real but mostly administrative, and the bill included technical assistance, waivers when local police refuse to cooperate, and small-school partnering options. On balance, the bill was a serious, bipartisan attempt at transparency, though some advocates would have preferred even stronger victim recourse than this version offered.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate education committee for five months, got one subcommittee hearing, and never received a committee vote or floor action before the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Senator Claire McCaskill introduced the Campus Accountability and Safety Act on July 30, 2014, with nine original cosponsors from both parties, including Republicans Orrin Hatch-adjacent figures such as Chuck Grassley, Dean Heller, Kelly Ayotte, Marco Rubio, and Lindsey Graham.
The bill was read twice and referred the same day to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
Seventeen senators cosponsored the bill — 7 Republicans and 10 Democrats — giving it clear bipartisan support.
The only further action was a December 9, 2014 hearing before the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Terrorism.
The bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or House action, and died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Colleges and universities are better off: they avoided new federal fines of up to 1% of their operating budgets, mandatory public reporting of how sexual assault cases were resolved, annual named-campus surveys, and required confidential advisors. Students gained nothing, since the protections never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Colleges that avoided new fines and disclosures

for.name: Sen. Claire McCaskill
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited bipartisan original cosponsors including Republicans Grassley, Heller, Ayotte, Rubio, and Graham.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-IA), senior Judiciary Committee Republican, original cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor at introduction.

for.name: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Terrorism
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the issues covered by the bill in December 2014.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Tom Harkin (D-IA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill during the five months after referral, and the full Congress ended without any Senate action on it.

against.name: Colleges and universities and their Washington associations
against.what_they_did: Publicly resisted mandatory fines, published case-disposition data, and annual government-run campus surveys during the debate over campus sexual assault legislation.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan at introduction — the bill's original sponsors included five Republicans alongside five Democrats, and 7 of its 17 cosponsors were Republicans — but no vote was ever taken, so the parties were never recorded on it.

industries.note: The bill would have subjected every institution receiving federal student aid to fines of up to 1% of its operating budget, forced formal agreements with local police, required named-campus publication of sexual assault case outcomes, and mandated annual student climate surveys — shifting real money and reputational exposure onto schools in exchange for transparency for students.

industries.industry: Victim advocacy and campus anti-violence programs
industries.note: Federal campus grants against sexual assault, dating violence, and stalking would have risen from a $300,000 to a $500,000 minimum, with funding allowed for trauma-informed interview training, and advocacy organizations could partner with schools to serve as confidential advisors.

The bill would have required colleges to sign memoranda of understanding delineating who investigates campus sexual violence and how evidence and information are shared, expanding coordination duties but clarifying jurisdiction in serious cases.
